\begin{abstract}
Bayesian optimization driven by human ratings is often evaluated against regression oracles fitted to archival data, which mixes the cost of noisy feedback with the oracle's own error. On the same landscape, such an oracle reports an eighth to a third of the cost the exact function shows. We instead inject four error processes into twenty analytic landscapes with verified optima, pairing each noisy run with an identically seeded clean one ($76{,}800$ pairs, twelve acquisitions). At the rater noise measured in three human studies, about $0.6$ to $1.1$ landscape standard deviations, the design a study would deploy loses $22$--$32\%$ of the achievable improvement on average. It loses on every landscape, and as much on an a-priori smooth subset. Those studies also show heavy tails and frequent scale saturation. Serial correlation beyond rater-specific drift is small where the data identify it. At one standard deviation, $42\%$ $[34, 50]$ of the loss is selection: the run visited a better design than the one it ships. No acquisition-side change we ran reduced the deployed loss. Changes to the final decision help on average, though not on every landscape: a comparative sitting over the last $k$ of $50$ trials, with $k$ chosen on other seeds, gains $0.017$ $[0.001, 0.033]$ of the achievable improvement on held-out seeds. Four confirmation trials cut false improvement claims from $16\%$ to $0.5\%$ but detect only half of the real improvements.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Bayesian optimization (BO) is the standard tool for optimizing an expensive black-box function from few evaluations \citep{jones1998efficient, shahriari2016taking, frazier2018tutorial}. It is increasingly pointed at objectives that only a person can evaluate: interface parameters judged for trust or aesthetics, generated content ranked for quality, robot behaviours rated for comfort, the setting of human-in-the-loop (HITL) optimization \citep{brochu2010tutorial, gonzalez2017preferential, koyama2017sequential, khajah2016designing, dudley2019crowdsourcing, koyama2020sequential, kadner2021adaptifont, chan2022investigating, liao2023interaction}. The optimizer assumes each observation is informative about the objective, but a person is not a sensor. People rate inconsistently, drift, are generous or harsh, make correlated errors, and sometimes apply the wrong setting altogether. How much that costs is asked routinely, and answered with a design that cannot isolate it.

A common construction fits a model to archival human judgements and treats it as the objective \citep{siivola2021preferential, astudillo2023qeubo, letham2022lookahead}, then injects synthetic error into its responses and measures the degradation \citep{astudillo2023qeubo}. Studies of learning from human preferences use the same design, with a reward model fitted to human labels as the gold standard \citep{gao2023scaling}. The fitted oracle is itself wrong. In the motivating studies its cross-validated $R^2$ is $0.55$ at best, $0.23$ when whole participants are held out, and negative on the other two once a logging defect in one and a sign error in the other are corrected (Appendix~\ref{app:archival}). The measured degradation therefore mixes the injected error with the oracle's misspecification, and regret is measured against a random-search estimate of the optimum that the optimizer can legitimately beat. The experiment also runs on one design space, so a result such as ``acquisition $X$ is the most robust'' cannot say whether it holds anywhere else.

We give up the human instead. On an analytic benchmark with a published optimum the objective is exact, regret is measured from the true optimum, and the geometry of the landscape can be measured before the optimization is run. Twenty such landscapes turn ``which acquisition is robust here'' into a distribution over problems, which we report landscape by landscape. Six of them, human-performance laws fixed as a smooth, low-modal subset before any result was computed, stand in for the objectives HITL studies actually optimise.

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}\setlength{\itemsep}{1pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
  \item \textbf{A protocol, and what error costs under it.} Twenty analytic landscapes with verified optima, four error processes at two onsets, and a model-free control whose excess search loss is exactly zero. At one landscape standard deviation from the first rating the deployed design loses $29.7\%$ of the achievable improvement, between $18\%$ and $47\%$ on every landscape; at the rater noise measured in three human studies, whose error processes we also estimate, $22$--$32\%$ (Section~\ref{sec:cost}). Holding the landscape fixed, the common fitted-oracle design reports about a quarter of that cost.
  \item \textbf{Where the cost sits.} Deployed regret splits into search loss and selection loss (Section~\ref{sec:decomp}). At $1\sigma$ selection is $42\%$ of the cost of error, rising to $83\%$ for a large error arriving late, and it is zero under exact observation. The acquisition-side changes we ran move both terms, and none nets a gain on the deployed design.
  \item \textbf{What helps, by how much, and what does not.} Procedures that act on the final decision rather than the search: a comparative sitting, a cautious ship rule, and confirmation before claiming an improvement. Every choice among variants is re-made on training seeds and scored on held-out ones. The gains are small, $0.017$ $[0.001, 0.033]$ of the achievable improvement for the sitting, and no single procedure survives a family-wise correction over the procedures tried (Section~\ref{sec:budget}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related work}

\paragraph{Bayesian optimization under noise.} Noise has been part of the formulation since \citet{jones1998efficient} and is routine in practice \citep{snoek2012practical}; acquisitions built for it include augmented expected improvement \citep{huang2006global}, the knowledge gradient \citep{frazier2009knowledge} and noisy expected improvement \citep{letham2019constrained, balandat2020botorch}. \citet{picheny2013benchmark} benchmark infill criteria under noise on analytic problems, the closest antecedent; we differ in treating the error \emph{process} and its onset as factors and in asking where the cost sits. Heteroscedastic and non-stationary surrogates \citep{kersting2007most, cowenrivers2022hebo}, outlier-robust likelihoods \citep{martinezcantin2018practical, ament2024robust}, corruption-tolerant acquisitions \citep{bogunovic2020corruption} and time-varying bandits \citep{bogunovic2016time} each model one of our error processes; we test representatives of the first two as remedies (Appendix~\ref{app:budgetneutral}). The regret of the best design visited and of the one recommended, simple and inference regret, are both standard in noisy-BO benchmarking \citep{picheny2013benchmark}; we measure their gap under rater error. Spending the end of a budget on choosing among visited designs is best-arm identification \citep{audibert2010best} and ranking-and-selection \citep{kim2006selecting}.

\paragraph{Human-in-the-loop and preference-based optimization.} Where the objective is a person's judgement the usual response is to change the observation model: pairwise preferences with an ordinal likelihood \citep{chu2005preference, gonzalez2017preferential, astudillo2023qeubo}, or queries a crowd can answer as a line search \citep{koyama2017sequential}. \citet{chan2022investigating} document what such loops cost and deliver from the user's side. A comparison is immune by construction to a strictly monotone fault shared across a sitting; Appendix~\ref{app:elicitation} finds that this buys a great deal against drift and nothing against a saturating scale.

\paragraph{Benchmarks and landscape analysis.} Results on analytic test functions need not transfer \citep{eggensperger2021hpobench}, so the landscape is our unit of replication, results are reported per landscape, and where the observational design cannot identify an effect we manipulate the geometry directly. Predicting algorithm behaviour from cheap landscape statistics has a long history in evolutionary computation \citep{weinberger1990correlated, jones1995fitness, malan2013survey}.

\section{Setup}

\subsection{Landscapes}
Twenty analytic benchmarks with verified optima, $d = 2$ to $11$: thirteen classical test functions, six human-performance laws including the Yerkes--Dodson inverted-U \citep{yerkes1908relation}, and moving peaks \citep{branke1999memory} (Appendix~\ref{app:descriptors}). The six laws are smooth with at most one interior mode, like the preference and performance objectives HITL studies optimise; we fixed them as the smooth subset before computing any result (Appendix~\ref{app:smooth}). Each objective is affinely standardised to zero mean and unit variance over its box on $2^{16}$ scrambled-Sobol points, so one grid of error magnitudes serves outputs spanning seven orders of magnitude, with the argmax unchanged. $\optz$, the number of landscape SDs by which the optimum exceeds the mean, runs from $0.76$ to $56.8$.

\subsection{Error processes}
\label{sec:errors}
Let $g(x)$ be the standardised objective, $t$ the iteration, $t_0$ the onset and $\sigma_e$ the swept magnitude, in landscape standard deviations. Observations are exact for $t \le t_0$. After that the optimizer sees $\tilde g_t$:
\begin{align}
  \text{\textsc{gaussian}}\quad & \tilde g_t = g(x_t) + \epsilon_t,
    & \epsilon_t &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_e^2) \\
  \text{\textsc{bias}}\quad & \tilde g_t = g(x_t) + \sigma_e + \epsilon_t,
    & \epsilon_t &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_e^2) \\
  \text{\textsc{drift}}\quad & \tilde g_t = g(x_t)
    + \sigma_e\tfrac{t - t_0}{T - t_0} + \epsilon_t,
    & \epsilon_t &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_e^2) \\
  \text{\textsc{ar}(1)}\quad & \tilde g_t = g(x_t) + e_t,
    \quad e_t = \rho e_{t-1} + \eta_t,
    & \eta_t &\sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(0, \sigma_e^2(1 - \rho^2)\right)
\end{align}
with $\rho = 0.8$ and $e_{t_0+1}$ stationary. \textsc{bias} is a generous rater, \textsc{drift} fatigue over a session, \textsc{ar}(1) a rater whose consecutive judgements are correlated. These are design choices. Appendix~\ref{app:archival} checks them against three archival studies, which show rater offsets and session drift of about this size (though the drift differs between raters). They show little positive serial correlation once each session's own trend is removed, so that \textsc{ar}(1) is a stress test. They also show heavier tails and more saturation than the main arms have, which the gross-fault and capped-scale arms model. We sweep $\sigma_e \in \{0.05, 0.25, 1, 5\}$ and $t_0 \in \{0, 20\}$ over $T = 50$ iterations with $5$ initial random samples, twelve acquisitions and ten seeds: $76{,}800$ noisy runs, each paired with one of $2{,}400$ clean twins (the seeds of every arm are in Appendix~\ref{app:estimands}).

\subsection{Optimizer and acquisitions}
Every arm uses BoTorch's default single-task Gaussian process (GP) \citep{balandat2020botorch}: a radial-basis-function (RBF) kernel with dimension-scaled lengthscale priors, inputs normalised to the unit cube, outputs standardised, fitted by marginal likelihood. Ten model-based acquisitions, five strategies in analytic, log \citep{ament2023unexpected} or Monte-Carlo form: expected improvement (EI, LogEI, qEI), probability of improvement (PI, LogPI, qPI), the upper confidence bound \citep{srinivas2010gaussian} (UCB, qUCB), noisy expected improvement \citep{letham2019constrained} (qNEI) and the posterior-mean maximiser (Greedy). There are also two model-free floors, uniform random and scrambled Sobol. Improvement-based acquisitions take the maximum posterior mean at visited points as their incumbent, the usual choice under noise and, as Appendix~\ref{sec:incumbent} shows, not a neutral one.

\subsection{Metrics}
\label{sec:metrics}
\textbf{The primary estimand is deployed loss}: the regret of the design a study would ship, the one with the best observed rating, at the final trial, minus the same in the identically seeded clean run, divided by the landscape's achievable improvement $\optz$. Appendix~\ref{app:shiprules} scores four other ship rules. \textbf{Search loss} is the regret of the best design \emph{visited}, $y^\star - \max_{t' \le t} f(x_{t'})$; at the final trial, deployed minus search loss is the selection loss of Section~\ref{sec:decomp}. Its post-onset per-iteration average, the \emph{trajectory} response, has lower variance and drives the acquisition ranking and several appendices, but it is bounded by the clean run's improvement after the onset (Section~\ref{sec:cost}). A final value is compared only with a final value. Paired runs share their candidate-proposal stream, and $y^\star$ is a verified supremum. Since a landscape SD is not a fully comparable unit across landscapes (Appendix~\ref{sec:currency}), every aggregate is formed from per-landscape values and every headline is also shown per landscape. Intervals are 95\% percentile landscape bootstraps; at twenty clusters they cover $92$--$93\%$, and a $t$ interval that covers $95\%$ is up to two points wider (Appendix~\ref{app:estimands}).

\subsection{Controls}
Three controls are detailed in Appendix~\ref{sec:controls}. First, the model-free floors never read an observation, so their excess search loss must be identically zero, and over all $12{,}800$ such comparisons it is. Second, no landscape is ceiling-limited by its clean run. Third, a uniform offset is invisible to a GP that standardises its targets, which \textsc{bias} at onset~0 confirms to within $0.012$ of \textsc{gaussian} at every magnitude.

\section{How much does feedback error cost?}
\label{sec:cost}

Table~\ref{tab:dose} and Figure~\ref{fig:dose} give the cost at every magnitude and onset. Error whose standard deviation equals the landscape's own, present from the first rating, costs the deployed design $29.7\%$ $[26.6, 32.9]$ of the achievable improvement. The best design the run visited loses $17.3\%$, so the design that ships loses $1.7\times$ as much as the search did, and $2.5\times$ at $5\sigma$, where the deployed loss reaches $71.1\%$. Figure~\ref{fig:perlandscape} shows the same cell landscape by landscape: the deployed cost is between $18\%$ (Rosenbrock) and $47\%$ (Hartmann-6) on every landscape, with a median of $29\%$ and an interquartile range of $25$--$35\%$, and every interval excludes zero. The six human-performance laws lose $32.7\%$ $[29, 37]$ against $27.8\%$ $[24, 32]$ for the thirteen classical functions, so the cost is not a product of multimodality (Appendix~\ref{app:smooth}).

\textbf{The late onset looks cheap on the trajectory for a mechanical reason.} There, $1\sigma$ error from trial 21 costs $2.8\%$ against $14.1\%$ from the first rating. But a noisy run and its clean twin share every design until the error arrives, so the post-onset excess can never exceed the improvement the clean run still makes after that point. In $27\%$ of late-onset runs at $1\sigma$ it sits on that bound throughout (Appendix~\ref{app:onsetbound}). The bound is $5.3\times$ smaller at the late onset, and divided by it, late error destroys $43\%$ $[34, 51]$ of the improvement still available and early error $41\%$ $[36, 45]$, a ratio of $0.95$ $[0.78, 1.20]$. The bound also produces the growth of the onset effect with the budget (in the budget arm, $2.3\times$, $5.1\times$ and $11.7\times$ at $T = 25$, $50$ and $100$, and about $1\times$ at each once divided by it). The deployed design is not bounded this way: there late error still costs $13.6\%$ at $1\sigma$, half the early cost.

By factor, the magnitude decides most: over its two decades it moves the trajectory cost from the first rating by $23\times$; within the $1\sigma$ cell the landscape moves it by $8.1\times$, the acquisition by $2.8\times$ and the error process by $1.3\times$. The last comparison is partly fixed by construction (\textsc{bias} at onset~0 is \textsc{gaussian} plus an offset the standardised GP cannot see), so it describes these parameterisations, not kinds of human error.

\paragraph{Is $1\sigma$ a lot?} Within-rater noise in three published human studies \citep{colley2025ehmi, jansen2025opticarvis, susak2026provoice} is estimated as a nearest-neighbour nugget \citep{cressie1993statistics} over ratings of close designs by the same participant and expressed in $\sigma_f$, the spread of each study's fitted objective. It is $0.74$ $[0.48, 0.97]$, $1.11$ $[0.81, 1.40]$ and $0.60$ $[0.00, 0.90]$ landscape SDs, with participant-bootstrap intervals (Table~\ref{tab:anchor}). As logged, the second reads $3.35$ and the third $1.02$: $40$ of the second study's $586$ ratings were logged on the raw instrument scales, and the third's composite entered a lower-is-better construct with the wrong sign (Appendix~\ref{app:archival}). Once both are fixed, neither of those two studies' oracles predicts held-out ratings, so their $\sigma_f$ is fragile: another model family puts the second at $0.67$. Participants are noisy from their first rating, so on the onset-0 rows of Table~\ref{tab:dose} these studies would lose $22$--$32\%$ on the deployed design, interpolating log-linearly. The nugget can understate the noise, and the within-session residual bounds it at $1.2$--$2.4\sigma_f$, where the loss would reach about half. It can also overstate it, since close designs are not replicates: halving the closeness radius lowers the \texttt{ehmi} nugget by $11\%$ and doubling it raises it by $39\%$. The anchor fixes the range of interest rather than measuring any one study.

\paragraph{Does a fitted oracle understate it?} The fitted-oracle design is the common alternative, and its own companion run on the three archival datasets reports a third to a half of the cost measured here from the first rating (Appendix~\ref{sec:fitted}). But three human objectives set against twenty analytic ones compare different problems. We therefore hold the landscape fixed and change only the oracle. For each landscape we build a synthetic archival dataset as an archival study would produce it ($37$ participants, each rating the first $20$ designs of a clean BO run once, with noise at $1\sigma_f$). We fit an oracle to it with the pipeline's own model selection and rerun the experiment against that oracle, with the error scaled to its own $\sigma_f$ and regret measured from the best value any clean run reached. On the deployed design at $1\sigma$ it reports $0.25$ $[0.14, 0.78]$ of what the exact function on the same landscape shows, less on $15$ of the $20$ landscapes (Wilcoxon $p = 0.014$). On the trajectory it reports $17.7\%$ of the gap between the optimum and a model-free floor against $57.9\%$, a ratio of $0.31$ $[0.20, 0.52]$, less on $18$ of $20$ ($p = 0.0003$). The ratios at $0.25\sigma$ and $5\sigma$ are similar or smaller. The oracles are not poor, correlating $0.84$ with the true landscape at the median, and their fidelity does not predict the trajectory ratio (Spearman $-0.13$); on the deployed design the better oracles understate more ($-0.50$). On the trajectory it does not even rank the landscapes: its per-landscape cost correlates $0.11$ with the exact one ($0.69$ on the deployed design).

\section{Where the cost is: searching or selecting?}
\label{sec:decomp}

Write $x^\star$ for the optimum, $V$ for the designs a run visited and $d$ for the one it deploys. Then
\begin{equation}
  \label{eq:decomp}
  \underbrace{f(x^\star) - f(d)}_{\text{deployed regret}}
  \;=\;
  \underbrace{f(x^\star) - \max_{x \in V} f(x)}_{\text{search loss}}
  \;+\;
  \underbrace{\max_{x \in V} f(x) - f(d)}_{\text{selection loss}} .
\end{equation}
Equation~\ref{eq:decomp} is an accounting identity and by itself explains nothing. It is useful as a pair of counterfactuals. Selection loss is what a decision rule that knew the true value of every visited design would recover without a single new trial, so it bounds what any change to how a study chooses can gain. Search loss is what would remain with that perfect choice, so it bounds what a better search can gain on the design that ships. The selection term is zero under exact observation (the best-rated visited design is then the best visited design). That is why it never appears in a noiseless benchmark, and why a study that reports the best \emph{observed} rating, as HITL studies do, is safe there and not here. As a check rather than an assumption, the largest selection loss over the $2{,}000$ clean runs of the ten model-based acquisitions is exactly zero.

\textbf{A large part of what error costs is selection, and how large depends on the error.} Against the identically seeded clean twin the selection share rises with the magnitude and with the lateness of the onset, from $31\%$ $[20, 44]$ at $0.05\sigma$ from the first rating to $83\%$ $[75, 90]$ at $5\sigma$ from trial 21 (Table~\ref{tab:dose}). At $1\sigma$ from the first rating the excess of $0.297$ splits into $0.173$ of search loss and $0.124$ of selection loss, so selection is $41.8\%$ $[34.1, 50.4]$; per landscape it runs from $4\%$ (Shekel) to $85\%$ (Powell) (Figure~\ref{fig:perlandscape}). Pooling every cell would give $61.8\%$, but that pool is dominated by the $5\sigma$ cells and we do not use it.

\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/per_landscape.pdf}
\caption{The headline cell per landscape: the deployed design's excess over its clean twin at $1\sigma$ from the first rating, split into search and selection loss (Equation~\ref{eq:decomp}), pooled over the four error processes and ten acquisitions. Bars are the deployed excess with 95\% intervals over acquisitions and seeds. Shaded columns, labelled in the legend, mark the six human-performance laws, the smooth subset fixed in advance.}
\label{fig:perlandscape}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Acquisition-side changes move both terms and never net a gain.} Six acquisition-side changes (augmented EI, Thompson sampling, a lower-confidence-bound incumbent, minimum-distance proposals, a slip-aware acquisition and redistributed rating effort) ran as their own arms, with the human trials fixed, each scored against the standard process on the same cells and acquisitions (Appendix~\ref{app:budgetneutral}). None lowers the deployed loss, and split by Equation~\ref{eq:decomp} they fail differently: Thompson sampling \citep{thompson1933likelihood, russo2018tutorial} raises search loss by $5.7$ and selection loss by $7.7$ points of the achievable improvement. Minimum-distance proposals lower search loss by $1.9$ $[0.2, 3.7]$ and raise selection loss by $5.7$, a better search that ships a worse design. A lower-confidence-bound incumbent, the one change that lowers selection loss ($2.2$ $[0.7, 4.0]$), raises search loss by $7.6$. Redistributing rating effort across trials raises selection loss by $4.6$ to $10.4$ points, only one interval excluding zero.

\textbf{Re-reading the same ratings recovers little, except where the surrogate fits.} Under \textsc{gaussian} error at $0.25\sigma$ and above, four other ship rules recover from $-1.4\%$ (the mean rating) to $+10.1\%$ (the posterior mean less two latent SDs) of the deployed cost. The posterior-mean maximiser recovers $+0.7\%$ $[-4, +6]$, although at $n = 50$ the GP's noise estimate has largely recovered ($0.85$ of the injected SD). On the six smooth laws that rule recovers $+11.5\%$ $[6, 16]$ and beats the best rating on all six; on the thirteen classical functions it recovers $-3.3\%$. The GP's fit says why. On clean runs of the ten rugged classical functions it reads their roughness as noise (fitted noise SD $0.30$ where the truth is zero, against $0.03$ on the laws). Its lengthscales are a third of a box width against $0.85$, and its $R^2$ at fresh points is $-0.24$ against $0.67$. Across landscapes its leave-one-out fit predicts the rule's gain at Spearman $0.62$. The posterior does not inherit the error in general. It is misspecified where the landscape is rugged, and misled by structured error, losing even on the laws under large late \textsc{drift} ($-15.9\%$; Appendix~\ref{app:smooth}).

\section{Which acquisition function?}
\label{sec:acq}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Acquisition robustness, ranked over landscapes within each condition and averaged over conditions, on the trajectory and on the deployed design. Excess is the cost of error as a percentage of the achievable improvement; absolute is the noisy run's trajectory regret. The floor's deployed excess is the cost of error to the design random search would ship.}
\label{tab:acq}
\input{tables/acquisitions}
\end{table}

On the trajectory the confidence-bound family and noisy expected improvement are the most robust and the probability-of-improvement family and Greedy the least (Table~\ref{tab:acq}); the Friedman test \citep{friedman1937use} over landscapes reaches $p < 0.05$ in $28$ of $32$ conditions. Counted at the family level, since the ten arms are five strategies, UCB has the best mean rank in $17$ of $32$ conditions and noisy EI in $13$. Landscapes disagree either way (median Kendall's $W$ \citep{kendall1939problem}, $0.247$ over arms, $0.233$ over families), so a winner found on one landscape largely does not transfer.

\textbf{On the design that ships, the ranking largely dissolves.} Ranked on deployed excess, the mean ranks span $4.9$ to $6.7$ rather than $3.9$ to $7.7$, the two rankings correlate at Spearman $0.59$, and Greedy, eighth on the trajectory, has the lowest deployed excess. With error from the first rating the model-free floors (random and Sobol, averaged) ship a design at $1\sigma$ almost as good as PI's and Greedy's ($52.5\%$ absolute regret against $52.4\%$ and $52.1\%$), and at $5\sigma$ a better one than four of the ten acquisitions.

\section{Buying identification with the trials you have}
\label{sec:budget}

If much of the cost is selection and re-reading the ratings recovers little of it, the remaining lever is to spend human trials on identifying rather than searching. Every procedure below changes only the end of a run, so each is replayed exactly from an existing log (Appendix~\ref{app:endofstudy}). Each choice we made among variants is re-made on seeds 7--11 and scored on seeds 12--16, with landscape splits as a second check (Appendix~\ref{app:heldout}, Table~\ref{tab:heldout}).

\textbf{A final comparative sitting.} We hold $T = 50$ and spend the last $k$ trials on one sitting: the top $k$ visited designs by the posterior mean less one latent SD are each shown once, and the best-rated is deployed. Error shared across one sitting cancels when designs are compared; the looks carry the full idiosyncratic noise. The gain over the standard process is an inverted U in $k$ (Figure~\ref{fig:kcurve}), flat at $+0.020$ to $+0.022$ of the achievable improvement from $k = 5$ to $16$ and negative at $k = 30$, against a hindsight ceiling of $+0.138$. Chosen on seeds 7--11, $k = 12$ gains $+0.017$ $[+0.001, +0.033]$ on seeds 12--16. As a share of \textsc{gaussian} error's deployed cost (LogEI, qNEI and UCB), the sitting over the top five recovers $12.2\%$ $[6, 19]$ on all seeds and $17.4\%$ $[9, 26]$ on the held-out ones, which score about seven points higher for every variant. It recovers $26.3\%$ at $5\sigma$ from trial 21 and $23.8\%$ under an unnoticed slip. Under misclicks, which cost little ($0.068$), it recovers $-24.5\%$ $[-45, -10]$: its fixed price of $0.024$, in forgone search and in looks that carry a rating noise the misclick arm otherwise lacks, outweighs what it finds, even with looks free of misclicks.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/kcurve.pdf}
\caption{Gain over the standard process from spending the last $k$ of $T = 50$ trials on one comparative sitting among the top-$k$ visited designs, in units of the achievable improvement, with 95\% landscape-bootstrap intervals. The dashed line is the hindsight-best $k$ per run. Pooled over the four error processes, magnitudes and onsets, LogEI and qNEI; the looks carry the full idiosyncratic SD.}
\label{fig:kcurve}
\end{figure}

\textbf{A model-based choice of $k$ does worse than a fixed one.} Choosing $k$ per run from the surrogate's posterior and the run's rate of improvement (Appendix~\ref{app:budgetrule}) gains $-0.005$ $[-0.022, +0.011]$, $0.027$ $[0.015, 0.039]$ less than $k = 8$. In $74\%$ of runs it ships the posterior-mean design instead, which on its own loses $0.013$, trusting the posterior the previous section found misspecified.

\textbf{A cautious ship rule, at no extra trial.} Shipping the visited design with the highest posterior mean less two latent SDs recovers $10.1\%$ $[4.6, 15.9]$ of \textsc{gaussian} error's deployed cost at $0.25\sigma$ and above, $10.7\%$ $[5, 16]$ on the held-out seeds, and $13.9\%$ $[11, 17]$ on the smooth laws (Appendix~\ref{app:smooth}). It pays a fixed price of $0.015$ whether or not error is present, so it should not be used without an estimate of the rater's noise.

\textbf{Confirm before claiming.} A study also claims that its design beats where it started. The standard process claims an improvement in $98\%$ of runs, and $15.7\%$ of runs make a false claim, $42.7\%$ at $5\sigma$ from the first rating (\textsc{gaussian} error, LogEI, qNEI and UCB). Spending four final trials rating the chosen and the initial design twice each and claiming only if a one-sided paired $t$-test at $\alpha = 0.05$ prefers the chosen one takes the false-claim rate to $0.5\%$. Of that $15.2$-point reduction the fresh ratings supply $9.1$ points ($60\%$) and the test $6.1$. The test is not free: claiming on the fresh mean alone detects $88\%$ of the real improvements, and the test cuts that to $51\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:endofstudy}).

\textbf{These are average gains, not uniform ones.} On the held-out seeds the sitting gains on $15$ of $20$ landscapes and the cautious rule on $16$. With a Wilcoxon test across landscapes and Holm's correction \citep{holm1979simple} over the $27$ procedures of that family, neither survives (adjusted $p = 0.09$ and $0.06$), nor does any fixed $k$ over all $41$. Of the fixes that spend no trials (Appendix~\ref{app:remedies}), choosing on the ratings' ranks recovers $51\%$ $[36, 63]$ of the cost when $15\%$ of trials carry a gross fault ($49\%$ $[34, 63]$ on held-out seeds) and nothing when none do. A self-reported confidence used as a per-trial variance helps only if the report tracks the rater's realised error almost perfectly. In the two cells where such a report recovers $31\%$, one with a rank correlation of $0.6$ recovers $12\%$ $[-1, 23]$, and at $0.3$ or $0$ the estimates turn negative ($-10\%$ $[-25, 4]$, $-16\%$ $[-37, 2]$). Shipping the top three designs would put one within reach that recovers $24\%$ $[18, 30]$ of the cost, a bound on what a later decision could recover rather than a remedy.

\section{When the error is in the design, not the rating}
\label{sec:inputerror}

People also make the other mistake: the optimizer proposes $x$, the person experiences $x' \neq x$ (a slider overshoots) and rates it honestly, and the rating is filed against $x$. This is the noisy-input setting of \citet{oliveira2019bayesian} and \citet{frohlich2020noisy}, except that the optimizer does not know the perturbation. A \textsc{slip} of $15\%$ of each coordinate's range costs about what one-SD rating noise costs. \textbf{The design in the log is not the design that earned its rating}. Scored where the log says it is, the deployed design loses $16.4\%$ of the achievable improvement at a $5\%$ slip and $65.8\%$ at $40\%$, $2.5$ times what the designs the person experienced lose (Appendix~\ref{app:inputerrorarm}).

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

At the rater noise measured in three human studies, feedback error costs the design a study ships $22$ to $32\%$ of the improvement it could have had, against a clean run that ships within $13\%$ of the optimum (the noisy deployed regret at $1\sigma$ is $0.425$ of the achievable improvement and its excess $0.297$). It would cost up to about half if the within-session residual were all noise. That is worth reducing, and it grows fast: at $5\sigma$ the model-free floors ship a better design than four of the ten acquisitions. Three consequences follow. Report the deployed design, not the trajectory, on which acquisition rankings and onset effects look different (the rankings correlate at $0.59$; the onset ratio is $5\times$ against $2.2\times$). Estimate the rater's noise relative to the objective's spread before the study: the magnitude decides more than the kind of error does, and a one-shot predictor computed from a pilot adds little to it on the deployed design (Appendix~\ref{app:mediation}). And spend the end of the budget on the decision, with a final sitting, a cautious rule once the noise is known to be moderate, and a confirmation test before any claim of improvement. Their gains are averages over problems, not guarantees on each.

Two things remain unexplained: why the cost grows with $\optz$ faster than a scale-free error would allow when $\optz$ is not causal on its own (Appendix~\ref{sec:manipulation}), and why the incumbent choice changes the deployed design in the opposite direction from the trajectory (Appendix~\ref{sec:incumbent}). The onset effect's growth with the budget is the mechanical bound of Section~\ref{sec:cost}.

\paragraph{Limitations.} The landscapes are analytic, not people; the smooth subset and the oracle-isolation experiment narrow that gap without closing it. The error processes' fit to human raters is checked on only three studies (Appendix~\ref{app:archival}), where drift and serial dependence are weakly identified, and the measured noise runs through a fitted oracle's $\sigma_f$. The remedies were chosen from families of variants; held-out seeds and landscapes put the optimism of those choices under $0.006$ of the achievable improvement for $k$ and $4$ points for the sitting, but the family-wise tests are the honest summary. Extra-trial counts are censored and tolerance-dependent (Appendix~\ref{app:extra}), the multi-objective arm cannot separate the hypervolume acquisitions, and the preregistered replication is void on a control failure.

\section*{Reproducibility statement}
Every table is generated by one script from analysis outputs, every analysis output by a script in the repository, and \texttt{paper/COMMANDS.md} records the command behind each; every stochastic component is explicitly seeded. Regenerating published LogEI and qNEI runs from their recorded settings reproduces them bit for bit, and the seed order of the model-based acquisitions has not changed since the sweep. The model-free floors of the main sweep do not reproduce their recorded noisy observations: their noise seed moved when two robust baselines were added to the acquisition list after that sweep ran. Their candidates and regret still reproduce exactly, since a floor never reads an observation. Some reported numbers do read those observations, through the design a floor would ship: the floor's deployed excess in Table~\ref{tab:acq}, and its deployed regret at $1\sigma$ and $5\sigma$ in Section~\ref{sec:acq} and the Discussion. They are what the runs recorded; a regeneration would draw fresh noise from the same distribution and give different values. The seed order is now pinned by test. Three further checks are automated. The vendored benchmark implementations are asserted by test to agree with their source implementations to $10^{-9}$ relative on random points, so the objective cannot silently drift. The model-free control of Appendix~\ref{sec:controls} is verified to be exactly zero in every run. And one recorded optimum in the source suite, the supremum for a superseded parameter setting, is wrong by $64\%$; we detected this by searching every box against its recorded value and corrected it here. A test asserts both the correction and the provenance of the original. Software and compute: BoTorch 0.18.2 on PyTorch 2.13 (a CUDA build, though the simulator uses the CPU only), Python 3.12 on Windows 11. A run costs about $21$ worker-seconds and the main sweep about $470$ worker-hours on a 24-worker machine. Code, run settings and the analysis outputs that every table and figure is read from are in the anonymised repository at \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/hitl-mobo-robustness-tests-17E2/}; the main sweep's run logs ($4.4$~GB) are not, since they regenerate from the recorded settings. The preregistration of Appendix~\ref{sec:confirmatory} is \texttt{output-boba-confirmatory/HYPOTHESIS.md}. It was written ten hours before the first confirmatory run by the files' own timestamps, but first committed to the repository together with the results, so its priority rests on local file times rather than on a public registry, and we do not ask more of it than the void-run rule it states. An archived snapshot with a DOI will accompany the camera-ready version.

\subsection*{AI use statement}
In this work, we used generative AI tools (Claude, Anthropic) for the following tasks with required disclosure: proposing and refining hypotheses; designing and giving feedback on the research methodology and the experiments; implementing methods, including the simulator, the analysis pipelines and the replay toolkit; generating the synthetic data sets that those simulations produce; cleaning and reformatting the archival rating datasets; helping to develop the conceptual framework of search and selection loss; and interpreting results, with the authors deciding every claim. We have not used generative AI tools for translation, and the formulation and proof of mathematical claims and qualitative or thematic data analysis are not applicable to this work. Additionally, we used generative AI tools for the recommended-disclosure tasks of drafting parts of the paper, editing it for readability, suggesting its structure, creating and editing software code, creating the scientific figures from the analysis outputs, brainstorming, and identifying and formatting a small number of references.

We have reviewed all AI-assisted work. AI-generated code is covered by an automated test suite that pins the estimands, the seed order and the negative controls against hand-computed values; two independently written pipelines compute the deployed excess and must agree before a table is written; every table is generated from the analysis outputs by one script; and the numbers quoted in the prose were audited against those outputs in three independent passes. The authors set the research questions, chose among the proposed designs, and take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

\subsection*{Ethics statement}
This work collects no new human data. The three human studies it draws on \citep{colley2025ehmi, jansen2025opticarvis, susak2026provoice} are published archival rating datasets, used here only to estimate within-rater noise and the parameters of the error processes (Section~\ref{sec:cost}, Appendix~\ref{app:archival}) and as fitted-oracle companions (Appendix~\ref{sec:fitted}); no participant is identifiable from any quantity we report. The original publications state that two of the studies followed their university's ethics-committee guidelines under local regulations that required no additional formal approval, and that the third received institutional ethics approval. In all three, participants gave informed consent, were compensated, and agreed to the anonymised publication of their data, which the original authors released openly. We use only those released ratings, within the terms of their publication. The analytic landscapes involve no human participants. We foresee no direct negative societal impact: the paper's recommendations (confirm a claimed improvement before reporting it, and spend part of a human-feedback budget on identification) reduce the rate of false improvement claims rather than raise it.

\section{Design, controls and estimands}
\label{app:partA}

\subsection{The three controls}
\label{sec:controls}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Model-free floor.} \texttt{Random} and \texttt{Sobol} never read an observation, so their excess search loss must be identically zero, and across all $12{,}800$ such comparisons the largest absolute value is exactly zero. The analysis raises rather than warns if it is not, and the table reads the value from that check rather than printing a constant. This negative control shows that no observation noise reaches the candidate stream. The floors are then excluded from the robustness ranking, which a method that ignores its data would otherwise win.
  \item \textbf{Headroom.} Where the clean run already reaches the optimum a null is guaranteed, not earned. The smallest clean-run advantage over the floor is $0.176$ (Rosenbrock), so no landscape is ceiling-limited.
  \item \textbf{Uniform offset.} A constant added to every observation is invisible to a GP that standardises its targets and uses a posterior-mean incumbent. With a shared noise stream the two arms propose identical designs to below $10^{-9}$ for the initial design and three model-based candidates (asserted by test), after which floating-point differences are amplified; in the sweep, \textsc{bias} and \textsc{gaussian} at onset~0 agree to within $0.012$ at every magnitude.
\end{itemize}

\FloatBarrier

\subsection{Estimands, intervals and seeds}
\label{app:estimands}

One estimand is primary: the deployed design's excess regret at the final trial over its identically seeded clean twin, as a fraction of the landscape's achievable improvement $\optz$, averaged within a landscape over acquisitions and seeds and then over landscapes. Every other number is one of five derived quantities, named where it is used: (i) the final-trial search loss and (ii) the selection loss, the two terms of Equation~\ref{eq:decomp}, which sum to the primary estimand; (iii) the trajectory response, the post-onset per-iteration average of the search-loss excess, used for the acquisition ranking, the predictor and the currency test because it has lower variance, and bounded as Appendix~\ref{app:onsetbound} shows; (iv) the share of the standard process's cost of error that a process change recovers, $(R^{\text{std}}_{\text{noisy}} - R^{\text{adapt}}_{\text{noisy}})/(R^{\text{std}}_{\text{noisy}} - R^{\text{std}}_{\text{clean}})$, a ratio of landscape means (Appendix~\ref{app:adapt}); and (v) the gain over the standard process in units of the achievable improvement, the numerator of (iv), used where the cost in the denominator is near zero or pooled over very different magnitudes, as for the $k$-curve.

\textbf{Intervals.} Intervals are percentile intervals from $2000$ landscape resamples. With twenty clusters such an interval is known to run narrow, so we checked it by simulation, treating the empirical distribution of the twenty landscapes as the population and drawing $10{,}000$ studies of twenty landscapes from it. For the selection share at $1\sigma$, the shortlist recovery and the deployed cost at $1\sigma$ the percentile interval covers $92.2\%$, $92.9\%$ and $92.7\%$ of the time, BCa $92.1$--$94.0\%$, and a $t$ interval with 19 degrees of freedom and a delta-method standard error $94.6$--$94.7\%$, at up to two points more width; for the selection share, with $20{,}000$ resamples, it gives $[32.7, 51.0]$ against the percentile $[33.6, 50.2]$ (Table~\ref{tab:dose} prints the $2000$-resample percentile interval, $[34.1, 50.4]$). The shortfall is width, not skew, which BCa cannot fix. The check cannot detect bias the empirical distribution shares, or dependence between landscapes, which share seeds by design. The currency test (Appendix~\ref{sec:currency}) is the only place the paper uses BCa intervals \citep{efron1987better}.

\textbf{Seeds.} Table~\ref{tab:arms} lists the seeds, landscapes and acquisitions of every arm. Procedures that change only the end of a run are replayed from the logs of the arm they modify and add no runs; wherever a choice among such procedures is reported, it is made on seeds 7--11 and scored on seeds 12--16 (Appendix~\ref{app:heldout}).

\FloatBarrier

\subsection{Does noise ever help?}
\label{app:beneficial}

A noisy observation can in principle help, by pushing an over-exploiting optimizer out of a local basin. At one seed per cell, $25$ of the $640$ landscape-by-condition cells had negative mean excess regret with $d_z < -0.2$, noise apparently improving the outcome, which is the kind of finding that invites a mechanism.

At ten seeds it is one cell: \texttt{michalewicz} under \textsc{ar}(1) error at $0.05\sigma$ from iteration $21$, mean excess $-0.136$, $d_z = -0.21$ over $100$ paired runs. One cell in $640$ is fewer than the fifteen or so that a null family of $640$ tests would flag at this threshold. We report it as a null and note the sampling-variability lesson: the twenty-four cells that disappeared between one seed and ten were all in the direction that would have made the better story.

\FloatBarrier
\section{The cost of error}
\label{app:partB}

\subsection{The conclusions under seven further checks}
\label{sec:robustness}

\paragraph{The surrogate's noise estimate is not the problem.} The GP's fitted noise is an eighth of the injected value over the first ten iterations at $1\sigma$ and above, yet giving it the true variance removes about $3\%$ of the summed cost over the eight cells, $-1\%$ at $1\sigma$ from the first rating, and survives correction in no condition (Appendix~\ref{sec:noisediag}).

\paragraph{The incumbent is part of the method.} The observed-max incumbent removes $20.0\%$ of the excess-weighted cost, $24\%$ at $1\sigma$ and $48$--$81\%$ at $0.25\sigma$ and below, and worsens the deployed design: robustness rankings rank acquisition-and-incumbent pairs (Appendices~\ref{sec:incumbent} and~\ref{app:adapt}).

\paragraph{$\optz$ is not causal on its own, and dimension is not inert.} Purpose-built landscapes show that raising a narrow optimum never measurably raises the cost ($-0.001$ $[-0.035, +0.036]$ at $1\sigma$), that a Levy ladder confounds dimension with signal strength, and that with $\optz$ fixed dimension still raises the cost at $1\sigma$ and $5\sigma$, $1.7\times$ $[1.1, 5.3]$ and $1.7\times$ $[1.4, 2.3]$ from $d = 7$ to $11$ (Appendix~\ref{sec:manipulation}).

\paragraph{Multi-objective BO is no more fragile.} On six BoTorch problems the dose-response and onset structures replicate and the four hypervolume acquisitions are indistinguishable. Early error costs a seventh of the scalar suite's at $0.05\sigma$, a third at $0.25\sigma$ and a half at $1\sigma$ and $5\sigma$, the intervals separating only at the two smallest (Appendix~\ref{sec:multiobjective}).

\paragraph{The budget matters, through the onset bound. The rating scale cuts both ways.} With the late onset held at $40\%$ of the run, the early-to-late cost ratio is $2.3\times$, $5.1\times$ and $11.7\times$ at $T = 25$, $50$ and $100$, and about $1\times$ at each once divided by the clean run's post-onset improvement; a discretised rating scale makes small errors costlier and large ones marginally cheaper (Appendices~\ref{sec:designchoices} and~\ref{app:onsetbound}).

\paragraph{The replication is void; post hoc, the claims hold.} Four preregistered claims ran on ten fresh seeds; one control failed, so the run is void by its own rule, and with that landscape excluded post hoc all four clear their thresholds (Appendix~\ref{sec:confirmatory}).

\paragraph{The fitted-oracle design reports a quarter to a half of the cost.} On three archival datasets it reports a third to a half of the cost the analytic arm measures from the first rating, but those are different problems. Holding the landscape fixed and fitting the oracle to synthetic archival data drawn from it, the fitted design reports $0.31$ $[0.20, 0.52]$ of the exact cost at $1\sigma$ on the trajectory ($0.25$ $[0.14, 0.78]$ on the deployed design), less on $18$ of $20$ landscapes, and neither oracle fidelity nor the optimum estimate explains the gap (Appendix~\ref{sec:fitted}).

\subsection{What makes an error big?}
\label{sec:currency}

Standardising every objective assumes that a landscape's own standard deviation is the right unit for its error. The rival is the improvement available, since a half-SD error is one thing when the optimum stands $0.76$ SDs above a random design and another at $56.8$. We fit the power law
\begin{equation}
  \mathbb{E}[R] \;=\; A\,\sigma_e^{\beta_c}\,\optz^{\beta_z}
\end{equation}
to the landscape-by-magnitude cell means of the raw excess regret $R$, using quasi-Poisson estimating equations, the Poisson pseudo-maximum-likelihood estimator of a multiplicative mean \citep{gourieroux1984pseudo, santossilva2006log}, which needs only the mean to be right and keeps the cells where noise helped (Appendix~\ref{app:beneficial}). If the spread is the right unit (\textsc{spread}), $\beta_z = 0$; if the error relative to the achievable gain is, $R = \optz\, h(\sigma_e/\optz)$, and for a power-law $h$ that means $\beta_c + \beta_z = 1$ (\textsc{gain}). Intervals are BCa intervals over resampled landscapes, the unit of replication for a landscape-level covariate.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Neither scale fits. Exponents of $\mathbb{E}[R] = A\,\sigma_e^{\beta_c}\optz^{\beta_z}$ fitted to landscape $\times$ magnitude cell means, with 95\% BCa intervals from 2000 landscape resamples and a jackknife over landscapes. $\beta_z$ excludes zero in every condition; $\beta_c + \beta_z - 1$ excludes zero in six of eight.}
\label{tab:currency}
% Eight columns overrun the text width at normal size. Set here rather than in
% tables/currency.tex, which is generated and would lose the fix on a rebuild.
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\input{tables/currency}
\end{table}

\textsc{spread} fails at both onsets (Table~\ref{tab:currency}): $\beta_z$ excludes zero in all eight conditions, so standardising an objective does not make error magnitudes comparable, and a noise level reported without the problem's headroom is under-specified. The cost also grows with $\optz$ faster than \textsc{gain} allows: $\beta_c + \beta_z - 1$ is $+0.36$ to $+0.51$ from the first observation and $+0.76$ to $+0.85$ from iteration 21, with intervals excluding zero in six of eight conditions, \textsc{drift} touching it at both onsets; ordinary least squares on the logarithm of the positive cells rejects \textsc{gain} in all eight. The power law is itself an approximation: a centred $(\log\sigma_e)^2$ term is negative in all eight conditions and excludes zero in six, so $\beta_c$ is an average slope over the four magnitudes. Neither verdict rests on it. With the four magnitudes given free levels, $\beta_z$ is unchanged, since the panel is balanced. With $h$ left free, a B-spline with four degrees of freedom in $\log(\sigma_e/\optz)$, the coefficient that $\log\optz$ adds to it is $+0.31$ to $+0.44$ from the first observation and $+0.64$ to $+0.73$ from iteration 21 (\textsc{bias}, where four degrees of freedom do not converge, gives $+0.57$ with three), with percentile intervals excluding zero in all eight conditions, \textsc{drift} included. The estimate leans on \texttt{shekel}, the one landscape with $\optz$ above 25; without it $\beta_z$ is $1.04$--$1.10$ and the gap $0.57$--$0.73$ from the first observation. Appendix~\ref{sec:manipulation} shows that $\optz$ is not what does the work: raising a narrow optimum does not raise the cost at any magnitude, and the dependence runs through how findable the optimum is.

\FloatBarrier

\subsection{The onset bound}
\label{app:onsetbound}

Let $s$ be the last design a noisy run shares with its clean twin, $s = \max(t_0 + 1, 5)$: the design at trial $t_0 + 1$ is chosen from exact data, and the first five trials are a uniform initial design. Write $r_n(t)$ and $r_c(t)$ for the two runs' search loss. A running maximum never gets worse, so for $t \ge s$
\begin{equation*}
  r_n(t) - r_c(t) \;\le\; r_n(s) - r_c(t) \;=\; r_c(s) - r_c(t) \;=\; B(t),
\end{equation*}
the improvement the clean run makes after $s$. The bound is exact given the shared prefix, and the prefix is shared in all $73{,}600$ model-based pairs of the main sweep and both budget arms: designs, true values and search loss are identical through $s$ and observations through $t_0$, and no pair exceeds its bound. It binds often after a late onset. At $1\sigma$, $27\%$ of late-onset runs make no progress after trial 21 while their clean twin does ($7\%$ after trial 5 at the early onset), and $43\%$ of late post-onset iterations with $B > 0$ sit exactly on it.

Divided by the bound, the late onset is not cheaper (Table~\ref{tab:onsetbound}): the normalised early-to-late ratio is $0.95$ $[0.78, 1.20]$ at $1\sigma$ against the raw $5.0\times$, and the bound ratio, $5.3\times$, accounts for all of the raw one. The same holds for every process and at $0.25\sigma$ ($0.85\times$ $[0.60, 1.25]$), and at $5\sigma$ the late onset loses a larger share of what was left ($75\%$ $[69, 80]$ against $63\%$ $[57, 69]$); at $0.05\sigma$ the excesses are too close to zero for a ratio to mean anything. At $1\sigma$, thirteen of the twenty landscapes lose a larger share after a late onset. The raw ratio invites the reading that an optimizer which has located a good region is hard to dislodge. The trajectory cannot support it: after a late onset the noisy run keeps what was banked by trial 21 by construction, and of what is still available it loses the same share an early-onset run loses of its own. The deployed design is not bounded this way, and in $61\%$ of late-onset runs at $1\sigma$ its excess exceeds $B(T)$. There the late onset costs $13.6\%$ $[11.1, 16.0]$ against $29.7\%$, a ratio of $2.2\times$ $[1.9, 2.6]$.

\subsection{The error processes in the archival data}
\label{app:archival}

The error processes of Section~\ref{sec:errors} are parameterisations chosen before looking at human data. The three archival studies contain enough repeated structure to check them: several ratings per participant in one session, designs that recur, and in \texttt{provoice} a counterbalanced crossover in which the same design is rated in both conditions of one sitting. A rating is modelled as the design's value plus the rater's error. The design's value is removed with a leave-one-participant-out model of rating on design, of the family the fitted-oracle pipeline selects, so that a participant's own ratings cannot fit their own residuals away, and every interval resamples participants ($2000$ draws). Table~\ref{tab:archival} sets the estimates beside what the simulation assumes.

\textbf{Two defects in the fitted-oracle pipeline's composites.} In \texttt{opticarvis}, $40$ of the $586$ ratings were logged on the raw instrument scales ($1$--$5$, $1$--$7$ and $-3$ to $3$) and the rest on the $[-1, 1]$ scale the optimizer saw. Averaged together, they make one design a spike about four times the height of the rest of the surface, which sets that oracle's optimum and its held-out $R^2$ and puts its noise at $3.35\sigma_f$ (the as-logged row of Table~\ref{tab:anchor}); on the scale-consistent ratings the noise is $0.67$ $[0.49, 0.85]$ with the oracle family selected before the fix and $1.11$ with the one the pipeline selects now, and no model family reaches a positive held-out $R^2$. In \texttt{provoice} one lower-is-better construct entered the composite with the wrong sign. Both are now fixed in the pipeline (the off-scale rows are dropped, the construct enters with a minus sign) and the fitted-oracle companion arm was rerun on the fixed data. Both defects touch only the fitted-oracle companion arm of Appendix~\ref{sec:fitted} and the noise anchor; the analytic arm and the oracle-isolation experiment never read these data.

\textbf{What the data show.} The design model predicts held-out participants poorly (leave-one-participant-out $R^2$ $0.23$, $-0.21$ and $0.08$; the pipeline's $0.55$ for \texttt{ehmi} comes from folds that let a participant's own ratings into training), and search progress rises with trial order, so drift and serial dependence cannot be fully separated from progress the model misses; the one estimate free of that confound is \texttt{provoice}'s crossover, which gives the drift entry of its column. With that caveat, the four main processes fare differently. \textsc{gaussian} noise of $0.6$ to $1.1\sigma_f$ is what the nugget measures in the pipeline's $\sigma_f$ (Table~\ref{tab:anchor}), though the nugget can understate the noise, and the within-session residual SD bounds it from above at $1.17$, $1.34$ and $2.37\sigma_f$ ($0.81$ for \texttt{opticarvis} in the units of Table~\ref{tab:archival}). \textsc{bias} matches in size: raters differ by offsets of $0.7$ to $1.4$ noise SDs, though whether an offset shared by every rater exists cannot be identified from ratings alone. \textsc{drift} matches in size but not in form: sessions drift by $0.4$ to $1.2\sigma_f$, but in both directions and by amounts that differ between raters, rather than on one common ramp. \textsc{ar}(1) with $\rho = 0.8$ does not match: the raw lag-one autocorrelation lies below what the same estimator reads under it in every study, and once each session's own trend is removed it is near zero in two studies and negative in \texttt{opticarvis}, so most of the apparent serial dependence is rater-specific drift. An $\rho = 0.8$ component carrying a minority of the residual variance is not excluded (a third of it in \texttt{ehmi}, with an interval reaching $0.62$), and the \textsc{ar}(1) arm is best read as a stress test. The data also show two faults the main arms omit: tails heavier than Gaussian ($1.7$ to $2.4\%$ of residuals beyond three SDs, against $0.3\%$), which the gross-fault arms model, and saturation, with at least one construct at its best end in $55$ to $83\%$ of ratings and noise that shrinks for the best designs as a bounded scale compresses them. The main arms have no bound; the capped-scale arm of Appendix~\ref{app:budgetneutral}, among the most expensive faults measured, is the realistic one.

\subsection{What the fitted-oracle design would have concluded}
\label{sec:fitted}

The introduction argued that fitting a regression oracle to archival ratings entangles the cost of feedback error with the cost of the oracle being wrong. To measure this rather than argue it, we run the data-driven simulator on the three archival datasets at the same error magnitudes, expressed in each dataset's own $\sigma_f$ so that ``$1\sigma$'' means the same thing in both arms.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{The same experiment, run against exact functions and against oracles fitted to ratings, under \textsc{gaussian} error. Percentages are post-onset excess as a fraction of the gap between the optimum and a same-budget model-free floor (the floor gap), the one normaliser computable in both arms. From the first rating the fitted design reports a third to a half of the cost.}
\label{tab:fitted}
\input{tables/fitted_companion}
\end{table}

The fitted arm has no verified optimum, so Table~\ref{tab:fitted}'s denominator uses the best value any arm reached, which is attainable by construction and so inflates the fitted fraction: the bias works against the result below. Three design spaces against twenty also widen the intervals. Two of the three datasets carried the logging defects of Appendix~\ref{app:archival}; the arm is run here on the fixed data, on which neither of those two oracles predicts held-out ratings (cross-validated $R^2$ $-0.09$ and $-0.07$).

\textbf{Across different problems, the fitted design reports a third to a half of the cost, and only from the first rating.} At $1\sigma$ from the first rating the known-function arm puts the loss at $99\%$ of the floor gap (cluster-bootstrap interval $[55, 155]$) and the fitted arm at $46\%$ ($[31, 75]$), a ratio of $2.2$, interval $[1.0, 4.4]$ from resampling the twenty landscapes and the three datasets independently; three datasets allow only ten distinct resamples. At $0.05\sigma$ the fitted arm reports $4\%$ ($[1, 7]$) against $10\%$ ($[4, 18]$). From trial 21 the gap closes: the intervals overlap at every magnitude, and at $1\sigma$ the two arms agree ($10\%$ against $10\%$). On the defective data the arm reported a third of the cost; the fixes moved the two defective datasets from $5\%$ and $19\%$ of the floor gap to $31\%$ each.

\textbf{The augmentation contrast no longer tests fidelity.} On the fixed data, turning off the jitter augmentation changes the oracles' cross-validated $R^2$ by at most $0.03$ (on the defective data it raised one by $0.29$), and rerunning the arm without it moves the fraction destroyed by $+0.017$ $[-0.003, +0.037]$ on \texttt{ehmi}, $+0.006$ $[-0.006, +0.018]$ on \texttt{opticarvis} and $-0.015$ $[-0.056, +0.020]$ on \texttt{provoice} ($800$ paired cells each, seed-bootstrap intervals). The isolation experiment below is the test of fidelity. The optimum estimate is not the cause of the gap either: it cancels in the excess, a difference of two regrets, and enters only the denominator, which biases the other way. The three fitted design spaces sit in the lower two thirds of the twenty-landscape spread (per-landscape fractions at $1\sigma$ run from $0.11$ to $4.8$; the fitted three are $0.31$, $0.31$ and $0.75$, above six, six and thirteen of the twenty), and with three design spaces the arm cannot say whether that is a property of human objectives or of these studies.

\textbf{Holding the landscape fixed.} Set against twenty analytic landscapes, three human objectives cannot say whether the gap above belongs to the oracle or to the problems. The isolation experiment (\texttt{scripts/oracle\_isolation.py}) removes that confound. For each analytic landscape it builds a synthetic archival dataset the way one arises: $37$ participants, the size of \texttt{ehmi}, each contributing the first $20$ designs of a clean BO run on that landscape, so that the designs cluster where BO goes, rated once with \textsc{gaussian} noise at $1\sigma_f$. It then runs the companion arm's pipeline on it unchanged: the oracle family chosen by the same grouped cross-validation over seven model families (gradient boosting for fifteen landscapes, extra trees for three, CatBoost for two), fitted with the same augmentation, the box taken from the data, the optimum estimated by the best value any clean run reached, and the error grid scaled to the fitted oracle's own $\sigma_f$ ($0.78$ to $1.21$). The exact arm is the main sweep on the same landscape, acquisitions (LogEI, qNEI, UCB, EI), seeds 7--11 and onset, and both use the floor-gap fraction of Table~\ref{tab:fitted}.

On the same landscape the fitted design reports a third of the trajectory cost at $1\sigma$ and $5\sigma$ and an eighth at $0.25\sigma$, and a seventh to a quarter of the deployed cost, less on $14$ to $18$ of the twenty landscapes (Table~\ref{tab:oracleiso}); on the six laws alone it reports $19.8\%$ against $40.3\%$ at $1\sigma$. The oracles are not poor: they correlate $0.45$ to $0.94$ with the true landscape at fresh points (median $0.84$). Their fidelity does not predict the trajectory ratio at $1\sigma$ (Spearman $-0.13$), and at $5\sigma$ and on the deployed design the better oracles understate more ($-0.55$ and $-0.50$ at $1\sigma$). The fitted design does not preserve the ranking of landscapes either: its per-landscape cost correlates $0.11$ with the exact one at $1\sigma$. The estimated optimum again biases the fitted fraction upward, against the finding. A likely mechanism, which we have not isolated, is that a tree-ensemble oracle is flat where the archival designs are dense, so that near its optimum many designs tie and a wrong pick costs little.

\subsection{The smooth subset, landscape by landscape, and the surrogate's fit}
\label{app:smooth}

The subset was written down before any result was computed, from the landscape definitions alone: the six human-performance laws, of which Yerkes--Dodson and the steering law have one interior peak and Stevens, Hick, Weber--Fechner and the power law of practice are monotone with a corner optimum. They differ from the classical functions in more than smoothness. All six are four-dimensional, and four of them have their optimum at a corner, which among the classical functions only Eggholder shares, on one face. A secondary split, also fixed in advance, separates the three classical functions that are convex or effectively unimodal on their box (Powell, Rosenbrock, Griewank) from the other ten.

The laws lose as much as the classical functions from the first rating (Table~\ref{tab:smooth}; a difference of $+4.8$ $[-1, +11]$ points at $1\sigma$ and $+1.1$ $[-11, +13]$ at $5\sigma$) and less when the error arrives late ($-5.2$ $[-10, -1]$ at $1\sigma$), where more of their cost is selection ($87\%$ against $65\%$). Nothing in the headline is produced by the multimodal functions. Figure~\ref{fig:perlandscape} gives the headline cell per landscape: the deployed cost has a median of $29.0\%$ and runs from $18.3\%$ (Rosenbrock) to $46.6\%$ (Hartmann-6), and the selection share from $4\%$ (Shekel, where the optimum is so narrow that the search rarely reaches it) to $85\%$ (Powell); it exceeds one half on seven landscapes.

\textbf{Ship rules on the subset.} Under \textsc{gaussian} error at $0.25\sigma$ and above, the posterior-mean maximiser recovers $+11.5\%$ $[6, 16]$ of the deployed cost on the laws, beating the single best rating on all six, and $-3.3\%$ $[-10, +2]$ on the classical functions; the three convex or unimodal classical functions behave like the laws ($+9.2\%$ $[2, 17]$) and the rugged ten do not ($-7.4\%$ $[-14, -1]$). The cautious rules hold up on both: the posterior mean less two latent SDs recovers $+13.9\%$ $[11, 17]$ on the laws and $+8.8\%$ $[1, 16]$ on the classical functions.

\textbf{The surrogate at $n = 50$.} We refitted the loop's own GP on $800$ runs, twenty per landscape, clean and under $1\sigma$ \textsc{gaussian} error from the first rating. The noise estimate has recovered in both groups ($0.84$ and $0.85$ of the injected SD), and the posterior mean does shrink the ratings everywhere: its error at the visited designs is $0.52$ of the raw ratings' on the laws and $0.67$ on the classical functions. What separates the groups is the fit itself, and it shows with no error at all. On clean runs the fitted noise SD is $0.03$ on the laws and $0.30$ on the rugged ten, where the true noise is zero, so the GP reads their roughness as noise; the geometric-mean lengthscale is $0.85$ against $0.34$ box widths; and $R^2$ at $256$ fresh Sobol points is $0.67$ against $-0.24$. Across landscapes the GP's leave-one-out predictive fit correlates with the posterior-mean rule's gain at Spearman $0.62$, and $0.85$ within the classical functions. Within a landscape the run-to-run fit does not predict it ($0.07$), so a per-run fit check would not tell a practitioner when to trust the posterior. Structured error misleads the posterior even where it fits: at $5\sigma$ from trial 21 the rule recovers $-15.9\%$ of the cost under \textsc{drift} on the laws, and $-9.6\%$ $[-22, +2]$ under \textsc{bias}.

For each noisy run we count the trials it needs to come within $1\%$ of the achievable improvement of its clean twin after $k$ trials, on the budget-100 arm of Appendix~\ref{sec:designchoices} (\textsc{gaussian} error, six acquisitions; Table~\ref{tab:extra}; every arm in Table~\ref{tab:extrafull}). Against a clean 25-trial study, error of $0.05\sigma$ from the first rating costs a median of one extra trial and $0.25\sigma$ seven; $1\sigma$ costs a median of $41$, the noisy run reaching that regret at a median trial of $56$, $2.2$ times the clean study's, and $39\%$ of runs never get there within 100 trials; at $5\sigma$, $70\%$ never do. Error from trial 41 cannot delay a run whose clean twin was already within $1\%$ of its trial-50 regret by trial 41, and $84\%$ of runs ($505$ of $600$) were, so the median of zero in the right column is structural. In the other $16\%$, error from trial 41 costs a median of $8$ extra trials at $0.25\sigma$ and $50$ at $1\sigma$, and $49\%$ of them never recover within 100 trials at $1\sigma$, $78\%$ at $5\sigma$; over all runs that is the $8$--$12\%$ in the table.

\subsection{Three design choices that could have produced the result}
\label{sec:designchoices}

Every number above was measured at a fixed budget, against an unbounded continuous response, using standard acquisition functions. Each of those is a choice, and each could be doing the work. The three arms here ran \textsc{gaussian} error on seeds 7--11 with six acquisitions (LogEI, EI, PI, UCB, qUCB, qNEI) or, for the robust baselines, the two named; every reference row is the main sweep restricted to the same error process, acquisitions and seeds.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Budget, with the late onset held at $40\%$ of the run in each case and the reference row restricted to the arm's own error process, acquisitions and seeds, so that budget is the only thing that changes. Percentages are the fraction of the achievable improvement destroyed.}
\label{tab:budget}
\input{tables/budget}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Budget, and why the onset effect grows with it.} Re-running at $T=25$ and $T=100$ with the onset held at the same fraction of the run gives Table~\ref{tab:budget}. Early-error cost is roughly flat in budget ($9.4\%$, $11.7\%$, $11.1\%$ at $1\sigma$), but late-error cost on the trajectory falls steeply, from $4.1\%$ at $T=25$ to $2.3\%$ at $T=50$ to $0.9\%$ at $T=100$, so the onset ratio grows from $2.3\times$ to $5.1\times$ to $11.7\times$. The rescaling that lets one budget speak for another is the bound of Appendix~\ref{app:onsetbound}: the improvement the clean run still makes after the onset shrinks from $10.2\%$ to $6.3\%$ to $3.0\%$ of the achievable improvement as the budget grows, and divided by it the onset ratio is $1.0\times$ $[0.9, 1.2]$, $1.0\times$ $[0.7, 1.3]$ and $0.9\times$ $[0.5, 3.4]$. The budget changes how much improvement is left when the error arrives, not what share of it the error destroys.

\begin{table}[htbp]

Only the noisy run's post-onset ratings are clipped and rounded; its clean twin and every earlier rating are exact and continuous, so each bounded row measures noise and quantisation together, and the from-it.~21 row measures an instrument that switches on at trial 21.}
\label{tab:instrument}
\input{tables/instrument}
\end{table}

\paragraph{A real rating scale, which cuts both ways.} The synthetic objective is unbounded and continuous; a person returns a bounded, discrete rating. The three archival instruments have steps of $0.55$, $0.54$ and $1.12\sigma$ and span sixteen to twenty $\sigma$, so the arm clips to $\pm 8\sigma$ and rounds to $0.55\sigma$, the two five-item instruments, in the study's own currency. Table~\ref{tab:instrument} shows the two effects separately, against a clean twin that is not discretised; we read only the onset-1 rows, since at onset 21 the scale itself arrives mid-run. At $0.05\sigma$ the discretised arm is six times worse ($3.8\%$ against $0.6\%$), because rounding to a $0.55\sigma$ grid is itself an error of about $0.16\sigma$ and swamps an injected error far smaller than the step; at $0.25\sigma$ it is still worse ($5.0\%$ against $3.8\%$); at $1\sigma$ the two are indistinguishable ($11.7\%$ against $11.7\%$); and at $5\sigma$ it is slightly better ($20.8\%$ against $21.3\%$), because clipping bounds how far one bad rating can move the incumbent. A rating scale is a noise floor at the bottom of the range and, at the top, a marginal safety rail.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Robust baselines. qKG is the batch knowledge gradient \citep{wu2016parallel} in BoTorch's one-shot form \citep{balandat2020botorch}; replication spends every second evaluation re-asking about the incumbent. Compared at a fixed number of evaluations, so replication buys averaging with half the designs. The standard row is the ten model-based acquisitions of the main sweep on the same error process and seeds.}
\label{tab:robust}
\input{tables/robust}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Methods built for noise do not recover the cost.} All ten model-based acquisitions above are ordinary ones run under noise. Two baselines built for it: the knowledge gradient, which values the improvement in the posterior \emph{maximum} rather than in any observed value, and spending every second trial re-asking about the incumbent. Scored the way the rest of this appendix is, against each method's own clean run, they lose less: $9.2\%$ of the achievable improvement at $1\sigma$ from the first rating against the standard acquisitions' $13.9\%$, and $16.2\%$ against $21.5\%$ at $5\sigma$ (Table~\ref{tab:robust}). That comparison flatters them. Replication re-rates the incumbent in its clean run too, which carries no information, and qKG's clean run is itself worse than the standard acquisitions', so part of the smaller excess is a worse reference. Scored against the standard process's clean run (Appendix~\ref{app:adapt}), replication recovers none of the cost ($-61\%$ on the trajectory, $-5\%$ on the deployed design) and qKG recovers some of it at the early onset ($+12\%$ to $+43\%$ at $0.25\sigma$ and above) but more than loses it at the late onset and in the design it recommends ($-32\%$). What remains is the information the error destroys, which is what Equation~\ref{eq:frag} measures.

\FloatBarrier

\subsection{Does any of this hold for multiple objectives?}
\label{sec:multiobjective}

The applied setting is frequently multi-objective \citep{daulton2021parallel} and everything above is scalar, so the generalisation cannot be assumed. We repeat the design on seven BoTorch problems with a published maximum hypervolume (BraninCurrin, ZDT1, DTLZ2, DH2, VehicleSafety, Penicillin and CarSideImpact), spanning two to four objectives and two to seven dimensions, with the four hypervolume acquisitions (qEHVI, qNEHVI and their log variants) and the same two model-free floors, under \textsc{gaussian} error, at five seeds: $1{,}680$ paired runs, of which $960$ are model-based noisy-versus-clean comparisons on the problems that survive the headroom screen below.

Standardisation transfers exactly rather than approximately. Each objective is mapped to zero mean and unit variance over a fixed scrambled-Sobol sample of $2^{15}$ points, drawn as for the scalar suite, and under a per-objective affine map the hypervolume scales by $\prod_m \sigma_m$, so the standardised maximum follows in closed form from the published one. We verify this rather than assert it: across the seven problems the largest relative error between the closed-form standardised maximum and a direct recomputation is $4.7 \times 10^{-16}$.

\paragraph{Controls.} The model-free floor is again identically zero across all $560$ such comparisons, so no observation noise leaks into the candidate stream in the hypervolume code path either. No run beats its published maximum hypervolume. Acquisition-optimization fallbacks total zero, which we report rather than assume: a hypervolume acquisition that fails to construct falls back to random sampling, and because that produces a plausible-looking curve rather than an error, the arm has to be read off the fallback counter and not off the plots.

\paragraph{One problem is dropped, by the same screen as before.} DH2's reference point leaves a $32{,}768$-point Sobol sample with a hypervolume of exactly zero, and its best learner does not improve on the model-free floor at all. There is nothing for error to destroy, so its null is guaranteed by construction. It is excluded. The remaining six pass, with Penicillin weakest at $0.197$, comparable to Rosenbrock at $0.176$, the weakest admissible scalar landscape.
